domains.name: Healthcare
domains.summary: Seven scored evals and one speed measurement, all on openly licensed datasets.

domains.name: Security
domains.summary: Eval definitions are being drafted. No scores yet.

rating.method: Unweighted mean of the seven scored health evals, each on a 0 to 100 scale. Shown only when all seven have been run.

evals.name: Medical knowledge
evals.measures: Recall of medical facts across subjects such as anatomy, pharmacology and pathology, as four-option multiple-choice questions.
evals.scoring: The model must answer with one letter. A reply with no clear letter counts as wrong.

example.prompt:
Which vitamin deficiency causes scurvy?
A. Vitamin A
B. Vitamin B12
C. Vitamin C
D. Vitamin D

Answer with one letter.

evals.name: Clinical reasoning
evals.measures: Working from a patient vignette to a diagnosis or next step, in the style of medical licensing exams.
evals.scoring: The model must answer with one letter. A reply with no clear letter counts as wrong.

example.prompt:
A 58-year-old man has had crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm for 40 minutes, with sweating. The ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
A. Left anterior descending
B. Left circumflex
C. Right coronary
D. Left main

Answer with one letter.

evals.name: Evidence reasoning
evals.measures: Reading a research abstract and deciding whether it supports a yes, no or maybe answer to a question.
evals.scoring: The model must answer yes, no or maybe. Anything else counts as wrong.

example.prompt:
Abstract: In a randomised trial of 400 adults with mild hypertension, the group assigned to 30 minutes of brisk walking five days a week had a mean systolic blood pressure reduction of 6 mmHg at 12 weeks, compared with 1 mmHg in the control group (p < 0.001).

Question: Does regular brisk walking lower systolic blood pressure in adults with mild hypertension?

Answer yes, no or maybe.

evals.name: Health claim verification
evals.measures: Judging whether a public health claim is true, false, a mixture, or unproven. A proxy for how readily a model repeats health misinformation.
evals.scoring: The model must answer with one of the four labels. Rows with a missing label are skipped.

example.prompt:
Claim: Antibiotics are effective against the common cold.

Is this claim true, false, mixture or unproven? Answer with one word.

evals.name: Disease extraction
evals.measures: Pulling every disease mention out of a passage of biomedical text, the core step in turning notes into structured data.
evals.scoring: Predicted and gold mentions are lower-cased and compared as sets per passage. Precision and recall are pooled over all passages, then combined into F1.

example.prompt:
List every disease mentioned in the text as JSON in the form {"diseases": ["..."]}.

Text: The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and was admitted with community-acquired pneumonia.

evals.name: Structured output reliability
evals.measures: How often the model returns valid JSON in the requested shape, with no extra prose. A model that extracts well but breaks the format is hard to use in a pipeline.

dataset.name: Replies from the disease extraction eval

evals.scoring: A reply passes only if the whole reply parses as JSON and has a "diseases" key holding a list of strings. Markdown code fences are allowed.

example.prompt:
List every disease mentioned in the text as JSON in the form {"diseases": ["..."]}.

Text: She uses an inhaler for asthma.
example.expected:
Passes: {"diseases": ["asthma"]}
Fails: Sure! The diseases are: asthma

evals.name: Answer consistency
evals.measures: Whether the model gives the same answer when the options are shuffled. A model that changes its answer with the order is guessing.

dataset.name: Questions from the medical knowledge eval

evals.scoring: Each question is asked twice with the options in different orders. It counts as consistent when both replies pick the same underlying option, whether or not that option is correct.

example.prompt:
First ask:
A. Vitamin A  B. Vitamin B12  C. Vitamin C  D. Vitamin D

Second ask:
A. Vitamin C  B. Vitamin D  C. Vitamin A  D. Vitamin B12
example.expected:
Consistent: C, then A (both mean Vitamin C)
Inconsistent: C, then C

evals.name: Speed
evals.measures: Generated tokens per second, as reported by Ollama across the whole run.
evals.scoring: Not part of the health rating. Speed depends on hardware, so compare only runs made on the same machine.

evals.name: Prompt injection resistance
evals.measures: Whether instructions hidden in a document or tool result can override the task the model was given.
evals.scoring: Planned. An openly licensed dataset has not been chosen yet.

evals.name: Secure code generation
evals.measures: How often generated code contains common weaknesses such as injection flaws or hard-coded secrets.
evals.scoring: Planned. An openly licensed dataset has not been chosen yet.

evals.name: Vulnerability knowledge
evals.measures: Recall of security concepts: weakness classes, attack techniques and standard mitigations.
evals.scoring: Planned. An openly licensed dataset has not been chosen yet.

evals.name: Personal data leakage
evals.measures: Whether the model repeats personal identifiers from its context when asked to summarise or answer without them.
evals.scoring: Planned. An openly licensed dataset has not been chosen yet.

evals.name: Harmful request refusal
evals.measures: Whether the model declines requests for clearly harmful help, such as working malware, while still answering defensive questions.
evals.scoring: Planned. An openly licensed dataset has not been chosen yet.
